topics.title: Importance, location and classification of industries

learn.hook: Raw cotton is worth a little; the same cotton turned into a school shirt is worth much more. Manufacturing is the magic of adding value!
points: Manufacturing means producing goods in large quantities after processing raw materials into more valuable products. It is the backbone of development: it modernises agriculture, reduces dependence on farm income by creating jobs in the secondary and tertiary sectors, helps remove unemployment and poverty, and earns foreign exchange through exports.
Agriculture and industry go hand in hand: agro-industries raise farm productivity, and industries sell farmers things like irrigation pumps, fertilisers, pesticides, PVC pipes, machines and tools.

Industrial location depends on raw material, labour, capital, power and market. Many industries cluster in cities to use shared services such as banking, insurance, transport, labour and consultants — these advantages are called agglomeration economies.

Industries are classified by source of raw material (agro-based, mineral-based), main role (basic or key industries like iron and steel that supply others; consumer industries like sugar, toothpaste, paper and sewing machines), capital investment (small scale or large scale), ownership and bulk and weight of raw materials and finished goods (heavy like iron and steel; light like electrical goods).

By ownership: public sector (run by the government, e.g. BHEL, SAIL); private sector (owned by individuals or groups, e.g. TISCO, Bajaj Auto, Dabur); joint sector (run jointly by the state and individuals, e.g. Oil India Ltd); cooperative sector (owned by producers or workers, e.g. sugar industry in Maharashtra and coir industry in Kerala).

example.q: A new textile mill owner must choose between a remote village and the outskirts of a big city. Why might the city be a better choice?
steps: The city offers a big market for finished cloth.
It has banks, insurance, transport links and skilled labour already available.
Being near other industries lets the mill share these services — agglomeration economies.
example.answer: The city, because it offers markets and shared services — the advantages of agglomeration economies.

learn.reallife: In Tiruppur (Tamil Nadu) or Ludhiana (Punjab), many garment and hosiery units cluster together to share workers, suppliers and transport — agglomeration economies in action.

learn.hook: The cotton in your kurta, the jute in a gunny bag and the sugar in your kheer all travelled from a farm to a factory first!
points: Agro-based industries use plant and animal products as raw materials: cotton, wool, jute, silk textiles, rubber, sugar, tea, coffee and edible oil industries.
The textile industry is the only industry in India that is self-reliant and complete in the value chain — from raw material to the highest value-added products.

The first successful textile mill was set up in Mumbai in 1854. Early mills grew in the cotton belt of Maharashtra and Gujarat because of raw cotton, markets, transport and ports, labour and a moist climate. Spinning is centralised in Maharashtra, Gujarat and Tamil Nadu, while weaving is highly decentralised (handloom, powerloom and mills); khadi gives home-based employment to weavers.

The first jute mill was set up near Kolkata at Rishra in 1855. Jute mills are mostly located along the banks of the Hugli river because of nearby jute-growing areas, cheap water transport, good railway and road links, abundant water for processing, cheap labour and Kolkata's banking, insurance and port facilities.
Sugar is another major agro-based industry; many sugar mills in Maharashtra are run as cooperatives owned by cane farmers.

example.q: Why did jute mills come up along the Hugli river and not near Mumbai?
steps: Raw jute is grown in West Bengal and nearby areas, close to the Hugli.
The river gives cheap water transport and the abundant water needed to process jute.
Kolkata nearby provides labour, banking, insurance and a port for exports.
example.answer: Because the Hugli belt is close to jute fields and offers water, cheap transport, labour and Kolkata's port and services.

learn.reallife: A hand-woven khadi kurta or a Chanderi or Kanchipuram saree comes from the decentralised weaving sector that supports lakhs of weaver families.

learn.hook: Every bridge, bus and bicycle begins in a fiery blast furnace that turns iron ore into steel!
points: Mineral-based industries use minerals and metals as raw materials: iron and steel, cement, aluminium, machine tools and petrochemicals.

Iron and steel is the basic industry — all other industries, heavy, medium and light, depend on it for machinery. It is a heavy industry because its raw materials and finished goods are bulky. Iron ore, coking coal and limestone are needed in a ratio of about 4:2:1, with some manganese to harden the steel.
The Chhotanagpur plateau has the maximum concentration of iron and steel industries because of low-cost iron ore, high-grade raw materials close by, cheap labour and a large home market.

Aluminium smelting is the second most important metallurgical industry in India. Aluminium is light, resists corrosion, conducts heat well and is malleable; it is used in aircraft, utensils and wires. Bauxite is its raw material, and smelters need a regular supply of electricity and raw material at minimum cost.

The chemical industry has inorganic chemicals (sulphuric acid, nitric acid, soda ash, caustic soda) and organic chemicals (petrochemicals); it is its own largest consumer. The fertiliser industry makes nitrogenous (mainly urea), phosphatic and complex fertilisers; potash is entirely imported. Cement needs bulky limestone, silica and gypsum. Bengaluru is called the electronic capital of India.

example.q: Why is the iron and steel industry called both a 'basic' industry and a 'heavy' industry?
steps: Basic: other industries depend on steel to make their machinery.
Heavy: its raw materials (iron ore, coal, limestone) and products (steel) are bulky and heavy.
So the name 'basic' comes from its role and 'heavy' from the weight of its materials.
example.answer: Basic because other industries need its products for machinery; heavy because its raw materials and finished goods are bulky.

learn.hook: Factories make the things we love, but they can also make the air smoky, rivers dirty and cities noisy — unless we control them!
points: Industries cause four types of pollution: air, water, land and noise.

Air pollution comes from gases like sulphur dioxide and carbon monoxide and from particulate matter (dust, smoke, mist) released by factories, refineries, smelting plants, brick kilns and the burning of fossil fuels.

Water pollution comes from industrial effluents containing dyes, detergents, acids, salts and heavy metals like lead and mercury (from paper, chemical, textile and dyeing industries, refineries, tanneries and electroplating units). Thermal pollution happens when hot water from factories and thermal plants is drained into rivers and ponds before cooling. Fly ash, phosphogypsum and iron and steel slag are major solid wastes.

Land pollution happens when waste and chemicals are dumped on soil; rainwater can carry these pollutants down to groundwater. Noise from machinery, generators and drills causes irritation, hearing loss and raised heart rate and blood pressure.

Control: reuse and recycle water; harvest rainwater; treat effluents in three stages — primary (mechanical: screening, grinding, flocculation, sedimentation), secondary (biological) and tertiary (biological, chemical and physical, with recycling); fit smoke stacks with electrostatic precipitators, fabric filters, scrubbers and inertial separators; use oil or gas instead of coal; fit generators with silencers and use noise-absorbing material and ear plugs. NTPC has ISO 14001 certification and uses ash utilisation, green belts and ash-water recycling.

example.q: A dyeing unit in a textile town wants to stop polluting the nearby river. Suggest steps in the right order.
steps: First, reduce water use by reusing and recycling it in successive stages.
Then treat the effluent: primary (mechanical — screening and settling), secondary (biological) and tertiary (chemical, physical and biological, with recycling).
Release only cooled, treated water — never hot or untreated water.
example.answer: Reuse water, treat effluents in primary, secondary and tertiary stages, and release only cooled, treated water.

learn.reallife: When you see a tall factory chimney with little visible smoke, it is probably fitted with an electrostatic precipitator that traps dust before it reaches your lungs.
